evals.prompt: I run channel at Thalloway Systems - we sell a data-residency platform into regulated enterprises. 210 partners: 130 VARs and 80 SIs. Right now everyone gets a flat 22% off list and nothing else, and our biggest SIs keep asking what they get for hitting numbers nobody else hits. Our average sales cycle, from the moment a partner registers an opportunity to closed-won, is 11 months. Build me the tier ladder. I'm thinking Silver at 18%, Gold at 22%, Platinum at 26% off list, plus deal registration protection and priority support at Gold and above. My CFO wants the whole thing costed before I take it to her.
evals.expected_output: A three-tier structure where qualification criteria are defined and backtested against the 210-partner base before any bundle is priced, the deal-registration protection window is sized from the 11-month cycle rather than a stock range, 'priority support' is replaced with a defined SLA, and each step up carries a non-discount economic benefit.
expectations: Sizes the deal-registration protection window at 75% or more of the stated 11-month sales cycle - roughly eight months or longer - rather than a stock 60-90 day window.
Names the 11-month sales cycle as the input that determines the protection window length.
Rejects or replaces 'priority support' as an undefined promise and specifies a concrete response-time SLA in its place.
Explains that an undefined support promise becomes an open-ended services commitment that support staffing must honor.
Flags that a ladder differentiated mainly by a few discount points plus a badge gives partners no rational reason to climb.
Adds at least one non-discount economic benefit at every step up, such as deal-registration uplift, back-end rebate, MDF access, or dedicated partner-manager coverage.
Defines qualification criteria for each tier before pricing any benefit bundle.
Requires backtesting the proposed criteria against the existing 210-partner base to produce a modelled headcount per tier.
Costs each tier's bundle as benefit unit cost multiplied by the backtested tier headcount, and checks it against that tier's modelled revenue contribution.
Warns that the base discount sits inside the signed partner agreement, so it is effectively irreversible once granted and needs legal review before it is offered.
Stops short of finalizing the structure and asks the user to approve it explicitly.

evals.prompt: Vestrabyte - observability tooling, small team. We have 34 partners today, mostly boutique consultancies. Our CEO wants a five-level partner program modelled on what he saw at his last company: Registered, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum. I've drafted revenue thresholds for each of them. How do I split 34 partners across five levels so that each one actually has somebody in it?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to fill five levels at this base size, a recommendation to collapse to roughly two earned tiers plus an unranked entry rung, and the base-size reasoning behind it.
expectations: Refuses to spread 34 partners across five levels and recommends collapsing to roughly two earned tiers.
Ties the two-tier recommendation to base size, naming roughly 50 partners as the threshold below which three tiers cannot be filled.
Names five or more tiers with overlapping criteria as a documented bloat failure - a ladder nobody inside or outside the company can explain quickly.
Allows an unranked registered or entry rung below the earned tiers and distinguishes it from an earned tier.
States that three is the default earned-tier count for a larger base.
Applies a reachability check to the top tier of roughly 10% or more of partners.
Warns against a top tier that would hold only one or two partners at this base size.
Asks at least one clarifying question about the current base - partner types, distribution, or revenue concentration - before finalizing the structure.
Does not treat the five-level model as workable simply because a larger company ran it.
Recommends revisiting the tier count if the base grows, rather than designing now for a headcount the program does not have.

evals.prompt: Korrindale Labs. 180 partners in the program: 71 resellers and 47 agencies that actually transact, plus 62 technology/ISV and advisory partners who never touch a purchase order - they build integrations, they refer deals, they co-market with us. Our current ladder is pure revenue: $250k for Silver, $750k for Gold, $2M for Platinum. Every one of those 62 sits at the bottom rung, and two of them told me last week that the program reads them as second-class partners. What do I do with the revenue thresholds so they can climb?
evals.expected_output: A separate track for the 62 non-transacting partners with its own criteria drawn from integration depth, joint customers, marketplace presence, and CRM-verified introductions, rather than lowered or proxied revenue thresholds.
expectations: Recommends a separate track for the non-transacting partners rather than fitted criteria bolted onto the existing revenue ladder.
Justifies the separate track by the non-transacting share of the base - 62 of 180, roughly a third - and by their desired benefits barely overlapping the transacting ladder's payouts.
Removes the revenue-threshold mechanic for these partners outright rather than lowering, proxying, or discounting the dollar thresholds.
States that a revenue ladder cannot rank non-transacting partners at all, not merely that it ranks them poorly.
Proposes ISV and technology criteria built from integration depth or maturity, joint customer count, and marketplace listing presence.
Proposes referral and advisory criteria built from accepted-introduction volume and influenced pipeline, both verified in the vendor's own CRM.
Rejects self-reported pipeline or partner-submitted figures as criteria for the referral and advisory partners.
Levels partners within their own track rather than ranking them against partners in other tracks.
Notes that revenue is a lagging indicator of partner contribution.
Acknowledges the standing cost of a separate track: its own benefit set, cadence, governance, and communications, permanent once launched.
Leaves the transacting ladder's own criteria intact rather than rewriting them to accommodate the non-transacting partners.

evals.prompt: I inherited the channel program at Bramworth Analytics and it's a mess. I have one partner-ops analyst. Five tiers - Authorized, Certified, Premier, Elite, Elite Plus - with criteria that overlap so badly I genuinely cannot explain to a partner how Premier differs from Elite. 44% of our 315 partners sit in Elite or above. The thresholds were set in 2021 and have never been touched since. Partners tell me the ladder isn't worth investing in. And our churn spikes every year in the month after we publish review results. One constraint: the benefit bundles are written into signed partner agreements through the end of next fiscal year, so I cannot change what any tier gets until then. Where do I start?
evals.expected_output: An explicit fix order across the symptoms, leading with threshold escalation, striking the benefit-differentiation fix as blocked by signed agreements, mapping the churn spike to cadence and grace, and placing tier-count collapse last while naming the condition that would promote it.
expectations: States an explicit fix order across the symptoms rather than addressing them in the order the user listed them.
Places criteria-threshold escalation first and justifies it as a spreadsheet change against data the program already holds that lands at the next review.
Notes that the crowded top tier and the unexplainable ladder are usually the same problem, and that the threshold fix addresses both.
Strikes the benefit-differentiation fix for this cycle and says explicitly that it is struck because signed agreements fix the current bundles, rather than parking it at the bottom of a list.
Maps the post-review churn spike to cadence, grace period, and communications - demotion surprise - not to the tier count or the benefit bundles.
Prescribes advance written notice, published decision dates, and an appeals path with a named decision owner.
Identifies the 44%-in-top-tiers figure as tier compression caused by thresholds not keeping pace with base growth since 2021.
States that the efficiency-based ordering ranks tier-count collapse last, and names why: it is a migration, a communications plan, and an agreement amendment.
Names the condition that would promote the tier-count fix anyway - adjacent tiers no longer differing on both criteria and benefits, or a migration already happening for another reason.
Accounts for the single partner-ops analyst as an effort ceiling when ordering the fixes.
Does not recommend collapsing the five tiers as the first action.
Applies a top-tier reachability target of roughly 10% of partners when setting the escalated thresholds.

evals.prompt: Quillstone Data. We've drafted new Gold and Platinum criteria and my VP wants proof before we roll them out. The plan is to randomly split our 260 channel partners into two groups: half stay on the current criteria, half get the new ones, run it for two quarters, then compare partner-sourced revenue and PSAT between the groups. Our growth team does this for pricing all the time. Help me design the test - sample size, what to measure, how long to run it.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to randomize tier criteria across the partner base, with the reason grounded in B2B channel tiers being negotiated and agreement-bound, plus a backtest, a pilot cohort, and advisory-council socialization as the substitute.
expectations: Declines to run a randomized A/B test of the tier criteria across the partner base.
Explains the refusal by the nature of B2B channel tiers - negotiated, relationship-bound, governed by partner agreements - not by sample size or statistical power.
Contrasts this with affiliate, creator, or consumer loyalty ladders, which can legitimately be tested across a large base.
Proposes backtesting the proposed criteria against the existing 260-partner base as the modelling substitute for the experiment.
Proposes a pilot with a defined cohort rather than a randomized split.
Recommends socializing the near-final structure through a partner advisory council before any public announcement.
Reports the backtest as a modelled headcount per tier and as a percentage of the base.
Checks where key partners land in the backtest, including advisory-council members.
Does not produce sample sizes, test duration, or significance thresholds for the proposed split.
Recommends a notice period and published decision dates ahead of rollout.

evals.prompt: Here's the criteria sheet we drafted for Nyquist Cloud's new three-tier reseller program - tell me if it holds up. Silver: 3 customer logos in the last year plus $50k of partner-reported pipeline. Gold: 10 logos plus $300k reported pipeline plus a signed joint business plan with a committed number. Platinum: 25 logos plus $1M reported pipeline plus the joint business plan plus attendance at our annual partner summit. We picked these deliberately because partners can self-report them in the portal and we don't have to touch the CRM.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of every self-reported and logo-count criterion, replaced with criteria the program records itself - sourced revenue, certified headcount, a retention gate at the top - each with a measurement window and data source.
expectations: Rejects partner-reported pipeline as a criterion outright rather than retaining it at a lower weight.
Rejects logo counts as a vanity metric behind documented pay-to-play failures.
Rejects the joint business plan's committed number as a self-reported, gameable input.
States the test explicitly: whether the partner can move the number without creating real value, or whether the criterion survives a disputed demotion.
Replaces the sheet with criteria the program itself records, such as sourced revenue from the vendor's CRM and certified headcount from a certification registry.
Recommends a retention or gross-revenue-retention gate at the top tier.
Admits deal registrations only when vendor-accepted, and only as an input to sourced revenue rather than as a criterion of its own.
Attaches a measurement window and a named data source to every threshold it proposes.
Derives threshold levels from what the program's already-successful partners actually do, rather than from aspiration.
Does not accept 'easy to self-report in the portal' as a reason to keep a criterion.
Drops summit attendance as a qualification criterion, or replaces it with an auditable competency or certification requirement.

evals.prompt: Feldmarsh Networks. One of our resellers closed a single $1.4M deal in Q2 of last year, cleared our calendar-year revenue test, hit Platinum - and has done $60k in the fifteen months since. Still Platinum, still on the 27% discount, still has a dedicated partner manager. Three other partners are in exactly the same position. We recalculate once a year in January off the prior calendar year's numbers. Base is 120 partners and most of them transact every month. Fix the measurement so this stops happening.
evals.expected_output: A rolling trailing-4-quarter window replacing the calendar-year test, a recalculation cadence moved off annual with monthly considered given the continuous transaction pattern, and a graced, noticed demotion path for the four affected partners.
expectations: Replaces the calendar-year measurement with a rolling trailing-12-month or trailing-4-quarter window.
Names the failure the rolling window prevents: one spike period buying lasting status, sometimes called tier tourism.
Treats the measurement window and the recalculation moment as two separate decisions.
Moves the recalculation off annual and identifies annual as the cadence that lets partners coast for eleven months.
Recommends a cadence at least as frequent as quarterly.
Considers monthly recalculation and ties it to this base transacting continuously, rather than dismissing it as too much work.
States the recurring effort the chosen cadence commits to - a recalculation, a communications wave, an appeals queue - rather than presenting it as free.
Plans a grace period before the four affected partners actually lose status.
Warns that demotion is the highest-risk moment in the program and raises switching intent, worst for the largest drops.
Requires written notice and published decision dates before any status change takes effect.
Recommends letting old achievements age out of the rolling window rather than accumulating indefinitely.

evals.prompt: Ardenhold Software. The new tier structure is signed off internally. When we backtest it against our 410 partners, 96 of them come out lower than they are today, including 11 that drop two levels at once. Four of the 96 sit on our partner advisory council. We announce at our partner conference on 3 March and want everyone moved onto the new structure by 1 April. Write me the migration plan.
evals.expected_output: A phased multi-quarter migration with the advisory-council preview moved ahead of the public announcement, an explicit grandfathering choice, a grace period, differentiated handling of the two-level drops, and an appeals path.
expectations: Moves the advisory-council preview ahead of the public announcement rather than briefing the council at the conference.
Rejects the four-week announcement-to-cutover timeline and proposes a phased, multi-quarter transition with published milestones.
Presents both grandfathering options - setting each partner to the best status earned during the review period, or publishing an explicit no-loss date - as a choice rather than asserting one default.
States that the two grandfathering options cost the same effort because both fall out of the backtest already run.
Warns that a single no-loss date concentrates all 96 demotions onto one day, while best-status-earned lets them land one partner at a time as each window expires.
Flags the 11 two-level drops as the highest-risk cases and handles them separately from single-level drops.
Cites that status demotion raises negative emotion, threatens identity, and increases switching intent, worst for the largest drops.
Specifies a grace period before demotions take effect, with one review cycle - roughly 90 days - as the default.
Handles the four advisory-council members explicitly, either by reworking thresholds or by targeted socialization before announcement.
Defines an appeals path with a named decision owner and published decision dates.
Requires written notice to every affected partner before their status changes.
Includes post-demotion churn measured against baseline partner churn as a KPI to track after migration.

evals.prompt: Marchetti Grid, 140 channel partners. The board committed publicly to a new partner structure going live by the end of this quarter - that's 9 weeks away, and the date is already out there. My partner-ops team is one person at 50% allocation, and there's no analytics support available before next fiscal year. Our partners transact across sourced, assisted and managed motions and honestly I'd love something that scores all three properly. What mechanic should the new tiers run on?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation against a points pathway this cycle, naming the deadline and the capacity ceiling as the two facts that remove it, with volume or engagement chosen instead and the condition for revisiting the pathway later.
expectations: Does not recommend a points pathway for this round.
Names the 9-week public deadline as the fact that removes the points pathway from this round.
Names the half-a-person partner-ops capacity and absent analytics support as a second, independent reason the points pathway is out.
States explicitly which of the user's own facts moved which option, rather than restating a generic default ranking.
Recommends either volume or engagement as the mechanic for this cycle, with a stated reason.
States that engagement is the default mechanic absent constraints.
Expresses the mechanics' relative effort in orders of magnitude - near-zero, a few weeks to stand up, a standing job - rather than in currency amounts.
Acknowledges that the points pathway buys the strongest ranking power and that it loses here on effort, not on value.

Names the condition under which the points pathway should be revisited in a later cycle, such as multi-motion partners combined with partner-ops capacity, disputed tier assignments, or a compounding mandate.
Warns that a volume-only ladder scores every non-transacting partner at zero, and checks whether this base contains such partners.

evals.prompt: Our CMO went to an analyst day and came back with a 3x3 grid - current performance on one axis, future potential on the other. She wants our partner program rebuilt around it: nine boxes, nine partner levels, and every partner gets told which box they're in so they know exactly where they stand. We have 230 partners. I'm supposed to have criteria drafted for all nine boxes by Friday. Can you write them?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to publish the nine-box grid as the partner-facing ladder, with the grid retained as an internal overlay, roughly three earned tiers recommended instead, and an alternative deliverable offered for the Friday deadline.
expectations: Refuses to publish the nine-box grid as the partner-facing tier ladder.
States that a current-performance by future-potential grid is an internal segmentation overlay on a public tier ladder, never a replacement for it.
Rejects telling partners which box they are in.
Identifies future potential as a vendor judgment a partner cannot compute or contest, failing the dispute test for a qualification criterion.
Names nine levels as tier bloat, well past the point where a ladder becomes unexplainable inside or outside the company.
Recommends roughly three earned tiers for a 230-partner base.
Keeps the grid in the design as an internal sanity-check on where key partners would land.
Proposes partner-facing, repeatable tier names rather than box numbers or 'Tier 2'-style labels.
Requires every published criterion to carry a measurement window and a data source.
Does not produce criteria for all nine boxes as asked.
Offers a specific alternative deliverable the user can bring to the Friday deadline instead of only refusing.

evals.prompt: Pelloran Systems, budget review next week. We allocate 5% of channel revenue to MDF across our three partner tiers, weighted to the top. Last year $1.9M was allocated and $820k was actually claimed. Nobody owns the claims process - it's been unassigned since our partner marketing manager left in January. Meanwhile our top 14 partners out of 190 drive most of our channel revenue and they keep asking for a named contact and hands-on technical training, which I've been telling them we can't afford. Finance wants me to cut something. What goes?
evals.expected_output: MDF removed outright because no one owns the claims process, with the partner-manager coverage and delivered training funded at the top tier instead, justified by that cohort's revenue contribution rather than by an efficiency ratio.
expectations: Recommends removing MDF from the benefit set outright rather than reallocating or trimming it.
Ties that recommendation to nobody owning the claims process, not to the size of the budget line.
Notes that roughly $820k claimed against $1.9M allocated leaves over half unclaimed, consistent with the commonly cited 40-60% unclaimed range.
Recommends funding dedicated partner-manager coverage and hands-on training for the top tier rather than cutting them.
Justifies that by the top cohort's revenue contribution covering the cost, and explicitly rejects a pure efficiency ratio as the right test at the top tier.
Observes that 14 of 190 partners producing most of channel revenue matches the expected concentration pattern of 10-20% of partners driving 70-80% of revenue.
Names dedicated partner-manager coverage and delivered training as exactly the benefits an efficiency ordering systematically starves.
Proposes at least one near-zero-cost benefit such as directory or marketplace listing placement, or internal-use (NFR) licenses.
States that an unfunded benefit lands as a liability and erodes trust in the whole ladder.
Assigns a named owner to any retained benefit that requires a recurring process to run.
Does not present cutting the partner-manager coverage or the training as the answer to the finance request.
